dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimension.title: Required/Incentivised
dimension.description: When Required/Incentivised, the game challenges require players to communicate (e.g. when there is essential asymmetric information), or incentivised through challenges that are made easier through it (e.g. coordinating combined actions for maximum effect).

dimensionExamples.example: Players have to organise themselves before playing

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: Players pursue the same goal (finishing the level/game)

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimension.title: Pings
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate by signaling specific things in their view (e.g. aiming at something and signaling)

dimension.title: Voice Lines
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific voice lines their characters have (e.g. "Enemy over there!")

dimension.title: In-Game Movement/Actions
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific movement or actions (e.g. shooting a weapon on the ground to notify others to pick it up)

dimensionExamples.example: Some tasks ask players to do the same thing at the same time (e.g., hold a point)

dimension.title: Coincident Collaboration
dimension.description: In coincident collaboration, players are accomplishing the same task together.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimension.title: Sequential Collaboration
dimension.description: In sequential collaboration, players have to do tasks in sequential order, with tasks typically assigned to different players.

dimensionExamples.example: The whole party progresses together (even if the save is stored in the device of one of the players)

dimension.title: Party
dimension.description: Party progression results from the contributions of a group of players that opted to play together, where part of the progress is solely associated with that group (not shared with the rest of the server or community).

dimensionExamples.example: Players control their own character, and nothing else.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: No selection exists that the game assumes (it attributes specific characters to players 1 and 2)

dimension.title: Arbitrary
dimension.description: Arbitrary means that all player entities are equal in their ability to act upon the world. If a selection exists, it is merely an aesthetic choice.

dimensionExamples.example: Outside of tutorial sections, a player's character can always do the same thing (i.e., shoot portals, pick up interactables)

dimension.title: Static
dimension.description: When the player's entity is constant throughout gameplay.

dimensionExamples.example: There is no mechanic that relies on the relationship between players.

dimension.title: Individuals
dimension.description: Individuals describes when players’ entities have no established relationship with each other, which affects gameplay.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: The game's enemies deliberately focus isolated players

dimension.title: Spatial
dimension.description: Spatial, inspired by Reuter et al. 2014, happens when the game forces or incentivises players to be at a certain distance from one another. This can happen in a variety of ways, for example, by creating a radius around which players cannot trespass or by designing mechanics that punish players that move too far away from the group.

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: Ammo and healing items are shared

dimension.title: Consumables
dimension.description: Consumables refer to items that exist in a limited amount and can be utilised by players to invoke an effect (usually existing as a form of currency, materials, or food) or are not consumed on purpose by players but support the gameplay (e.g., health, energy). Consumables are shared when the agency to consume and manage them pertains to more than one player.

dimension.title: Interactables
dimension.description: Interactables refer to virtual objects and non-player characters/entities within the environment that respond to players’ actions. Interactables can be moved, shaped, or activated (e.g., a cannon that shoots when the player interacts with it). In some cases, interactables are also consumable (e.g., food in Overcooked is transported and modified as an interactable, but also consumed to complete the recipes). Interactables are shared when their state and attributes can be affected by more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: Some items are explosive and can damage friendly players

dimension.title: Space
dimension.description: Space is also a resource as it defines the various places in the environment that a player can occupy and interact with. Space is shared when its utilisation is affected or constrained by others' presence or by others’ actions.
